title: I Spent $1.2M To Be In Rooms Before I Asked The Right Question
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Summer Mulder traces the roughly $1.2 million she spent over the life of a business on masterminds, coaches, and paid rooms, arguing the first one was genuinely worth it while the pattern it created was not fully understood until years later. She names five stages the pattern moved through: the first room's real payoff, a quiet shift from asking 'what should we do' to 'who can I ask,' spending money as a substitute for making a decision she already knew the answer to, renewing memberships out of relationship attachment rather than continued value, and finally discovering the real avoided question - that she no longer wanted to run the company at all. Her central claim is that no amount of paid advice could surface that final question, because she was asking rooms full of smart people how to fix the business rather than asking herself whether she wanted to keep it. The piece closes with her decision to close the business while it was still profitable, framing that as the outcome only a self-directed question, not an outsourced one, could produce.
points: Distinguishes a paid room's real value (access to people ahead of you, occasional clients) from the habit it quietly installs - replacing 'what should we do' with 'who can I ask' - as two separate effects that most people never separate.

Names 'you buy instead of decide' as a specific failure mode where paying for advice on a decision you already know the answer to functions as a way to defer that decision another quarter, disguised as taking action.

Identifies membership renewal as often driven by relationship attachment to people who know your numbers rather than ongoing value, explicitly naming the conflation of the two as something that took years to untangle.

Locates the real, long-avoided question - not 'how do I fix this' but 'do I still want this' - as one no amount of external advice could surface, because it was never the question being asked of the room.
Frames closing a still-profitable business as the correct outcome of finally asking the self-directed question, positioning it as a deliberate exit rather than a failure.
quotes: Over the life of that business I spent about $1.2 million on masterminds, coaches, programs and rooms. Some of it was excellent. The rest took me until I was 47 years old to understand.
I stopped asking what should we do here. I started asking who can I ask about this. Small change in language. Total change in how a business runs.
I already knew what to do about most of it. Not everything, but most. Spending the money felt like doing something, so I'd do it, and the decision would move another quarter down the calendar.
At some point the renewal stops being a business decision. It becomes a relationship you don't want to end, and you tell yourself that's the same thing as value. Took me years to separate those.
It took until the last year or so for the real question to show up. When it did, it was that I didn't want to run the company anymore.
A million dollars of very smart people couldn't tell me that, because I never asked it as a question. I asked how do I fix this. The answer was I don't.
I asked how do I fix this. The answer was I don't. I closed it while it was still making money.
